newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German EMU strains grow with new jobs data.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German EMU strains grow with new jobs data.

text.p: Germany's jobless rate rose in April, throwing further into doubt its ability to meet economic convergence criteria for the single European currency in 1999.

Figures from the Federal Labour Office on Tuesday showed that German unemployment rose by 8,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.299 million in April, maintaining joblessness around current post-war record levels.

While politically-sensitive unadjusted unemployment fell to 4.347 million in April from 4.477 million in March, giving a jobless rate of 11.3 percent, economists called the figures disappointing and said they would increase pressure on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government.

"The figures will put more pressure on the government, throwing their forecast for a 2.9 percent (ratio of 1997 budget deficit to gross domestic product) yet further into question," said Hans Guenter Redeker at Chase Investments.

With key tax revenue estimates due later this month expected to show a widening shortfall in German state finances, Redeker said the government would be forced into more unpopular cost-cutting measures even to get close to the three percent deficit ceiling required to enter the single currency.

Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, a council member of the German Bundesbank, said late on Monday that the May estimate for German tax revenues would imply a German budget deficit of between 3.2 and 3.5 percent of GDP.

While the increased social welfare spending related to an added 8,000 workers on the dole is relatively slight, analysts such as Redeker are expecting a substantial tax shortfall of between 12-14 billion marks ($7.0-8.1 billion) compared to last autumn's revenues.
Bonn itself puts the shortfall at around eight billion marks but admits that figure might have to be revised upwards.
Government officials nonetheless seized on the new fall in the unadjusted rate of unemployment as good news for jobs.
"We can achieve a turnaround in the jobs market. The new figures show that," said Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats.
But the main opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said the data were fresh evidence that the government's forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth this year was shaky.
"There would have to be a miracle to still achieve such annual average growth," said Ernst Schwanhold, economic spokesman for the SPD parliamentary group. "
Bernhard Jagoda, head of the Federal Labour Office, suggested that government interpretations of the unemployment data were too optimistic.
"Economic growth in the German economy is too weak to encourage an increase in the number of jobs," Jagoda told a news conference in Nuremberg.

In western Germany, the number of people out of work on a seasonally adjusted basis rose by 6,000 in April to 3.016 million. Eastern Germany added 2,000 to unemployment rolls, reaching a total 1.284 million.
The unemployment data came amid other contrasting indicators on the strength of the economy.
Industry orders for March showed a greater-than-expected rise of 1.1 percent compared with February, boosted by a sharp 7.4 percent growth in the formerly-communist east Germany.
But economists were wary about extrapolating underlying growth in the economy from the figures, saying most growth was still coming from foreign demand for German goods.
"Exports are the driving force for the economy, not domestic demand," said Uwe Angenendt, an economist at BHF-BANK.

They were similarly cautious about the publication of a new indicator, the BME/Reuters German Purchasing Managers' Index for April, which showed a seasonally-adjusted rise to 56.58 from 54.58 in March, reaching its highest level since calculations began 12 months ago.
"These figures make us more confident in our forecast that the German economy is set for quite a jump in the second quarter," Larry Anderson, head of research at Bayerische Vereinsbank said.

"But we would be sceptical of saying that things are booming in the German economy. Exports -- BMWs, Volkswagens and so on -- are doing okay but this probably overstates the growth in the economy as a whole".
